title: Tables, keys, relationships
story:
Store data in the shape one program wants and the next program wanting a different shape is stuck, and every application ends up knowing how the bytes are laid out. Codd's paper of 1970 opens on that problem rather than on tables, and reading it in that order makes the model make sense.

The opening argument is data independence: future users of large data banks must be protected from having to know how the data is organised in the machine, and the activities of users at terminals and most application programs should remain unaffected when the internal representation of data is changed and even when some aspects of the external representation are changed. He notes that changes in representation will often be needed as query, update and report traffic changes and as the types of stored information grow. The model — relations in a normal form, with a designated key, and a universal data sublanguage for asking questions of them — is the machinery that delivers that protection, not the point of it.

Three pieces do the work, and it is worth being exact about each.

A relation is a set of rows over named columns, and set is meaningful: there is no inherent order, so anything depending on the order rows come back is depending on an accident rather than on the data. A key is the column or combination identifying the thing a row is about rather than the record — which is the distinction that makes counting possible, as the lesson on duplicates argued at length. And a relationship is not a pointer or a nesting; it is one relation carrying a value that matches a key in another. Nothing is embedded inside anything, which is exactly what lets a new query assemble a shape nobody anticipated.

The cost is real and worth stating plainly rather than defending. Assembling shapes at read time means joining, and joining is work done per query. Normalisation removes redundancy by splitting facts apart, and splitting facts apart is precisely what creates the need to put them back together. So the model trades write-time simplicity and storage for read-time flexibility, and when the read pattern is known, fixed and hot, that trade can go the other way — which is what the lesson on deliberately breaking schema design is about.

What you should not trade away casually is the key. Storage layouts change, denormalisation is often correct, and a table without a reliable identity for the thing each row describes stops being able to answer how many, which is usually the question that mattered.

problem.name: The relational model
problem.shape: Data stored in the shape one program wants becomes unusable to the next program that wants a different shape.
tell: applications know how storage is physically organised
the same fact is written in several places and they disagree
a query needs a shape nobody anticipated when the data was written
code depends on the order rows are returned in
problem.move: Store facts as relations with a declared key identifying the thing each row is about, relate them by value rather than by embedding, and let queries assemble whatever shape is needed at read time. Assert key uniqueness so violations stop the pipeline, and order results explicitly whenever order matters.
problem.invariant: A relation is a set of rows over named columns, with a key identifying the entity rather than the record, and relationships are values matching keys rather than embedded structure.
problem.breaks: Normalisation buys flexibility with joins, and joins are paid per query. Where the read pattern is known, fixed and hot, that trade inverts — which is why deliberate denormalisation is a legitimate design rather than a failure to understand the model.

cost.time: a join per relationship at read time, repeated on every query
cost.space: less than storing the same fact repeatedly, which is what normalisation removes
cost.beats: embedding data inside the structure one program wants, which is fast for that program and unusable for the next

worked.problem: What was the relational model actually protecting its users from?
worked.reasoning:
From having to know how the data is physically organised — and the reason that mattered is change rather than convenience.

The opening argument of the 1970 paper is data independence: users of large data banks must be protected from having to know how the data is organised in the machine, and the activities of users at terminals and most application programs should remain unaffected when the internal representation is changed, and even when some aspects of the external representation are changed.

The justification is the interesting half. Codd notes that changes in representation will often be needed as query, update and report traffic changes and as the types of stored information grow. So this is not an aesthetic preference for clean separation. It is an observation that the physical layout will have to change repeatedly over a system's life, and that if applications encode knowledge of that layout, every such change breaks every application. The model is a mechanism for making the storage layout a private decision.

Everything else follows from that goal. Relations rather than nested structures, because nesting bakes one access path into the data and makes the others expensive. Relationships expressed as values matching keys rather than as pointers, because a pointer is a physical detail and a matching value is not. A declarative query language, because saying what you want rather than how to fetch it is what leaves the system free to change how it fetches. Indexes as a separate concern entirely, which is the next lesson — they change performance without changing meaning, and that is only possible because meaning was never tied to layout.

The cost is worth stating honestly rather than defending. Assembling shapes at read time means joining, and joins are work per query. Normalisation removes redundancy by splitting facts apart, which is exactly what creates the need to rejoin them. So the trade is write-time simplicity and storage for read-time flexibility, and when a read pattern is known, fixed and hot, the trade can correctly go the other way.

The thing I would not trade casually is the key. Layouts can change and denormalisation is often right, but a table with no reliable identity for the thing each row is about cannot answer how many — and as the duplicates lesson argued, that means you are counting records and hoping they correspond to entities.

problem.practice: Take a table you own and try to state its key in one sentence — the thing a row is about, not the column that happens to be unique. Then assert that key's uniqueness against the live data. Separately, find a query in your code that relies on row order without an explicit ordering.

beats.cost: Assembling shapes at read time means joining, which is work per query — and the normalisation that removes redundancy is exactly what creates the need for those joins.

interview.q: What was the relational model actually protecting its users from?
interview.trap: Answering redundancy or inconsistency. Those are consequences; the stated problem is that applications should survive changes to the internal representation, which will be needed repeatedly as traffic and stored types grow.
